GROUNDING RULES FOR THIS ANSWER — these override any instinct to be helpful:

- Answer ONLY from this notebook's sources. For every number, band, or named
  standard, give the SOURCE TITLE it came from.
- If the sources do not cover an item, write "NOT IN SOURCES" for that item and
  move on. That is a correct and useful answer. Do NOT fill the gap from general
  knowledge — a number from model memory is indistinguishable from a sourced one
  once it is written down, and it will be trusted.
- Do not volunteer building-code or statutory values from memory under any
  circumstances; if a source states one, quote it and name the source.
- Prefer ranges with units (mm, lux, lm/m, K, g/m², degrees, ΔE) over adjectives.
- Where two sources disagree, show both and name each — do not average them.

CONTEXT: An interior studio working in the Thai market needs SOURCED colour and
reflectance anchors for a cream / oak / black palette, to replace design-intent
values that were chosen by eye and have never been traceable to a measurement. A
ΔE00 gate exists and has never scored, because the anchor file it consumes has
never been written. Numbers without a source URL are quarantined and do not enter
the knowledge base — please respect that: a URL per value or an explicit
"NO SOURCED VALUE FOUND".

QUESTIONS:

1. For Thai-market interior emulsion lines (TOA, Beger, Jotun Thailand, Nippon
Paint Thailand), which published cream / off-white colour codes carry manufacturer
LRV values in roughly the 75–90 band, and what are the exact LRV and hex/sRGB (or
NCS) values per code? Give the manufacturer page URL each value came from.

2. What is the published relationship between paint LRV and CIE luminance Y /
linear reflectance, and the accepted procedure to derive an sRGB base-colour triple
from an LRV plus a hue description? Cite the formula's source (standard, paper, or
manufacturer technical note), including the sRGB transfer function used.

3. What base-colour ranges (sRGB or CIE L*a*b*) and roughness ranges do scan-based
PBR material libraries and published references report for white/European oak
veneer under (a) clear matte lacquer and (b) hardwax oil? Source URL per value.
Name the libraries.

4. What 60° gloss-unit bands do architectural powder-coat suppliers publish for
matte, satin and gloss black, and is there any sourced conversion from gloss units
(GU at 60°) to a microfacet/GGX roughness value? If the conversion exists only as
practitioner rule-of-thumb, say so and give the strongest published form of it.

5. What measured complex refractive index (n,k) or F0 values exist for brass —
polished vs brushed/satin — and what base colour, roughness and anisotropy ranges
do measured material libraries publish for satin brass hardware? Source URL per
value; name the measurement database.

6. What L* / sRGB band do measured references give for architectural powder-coat
black and near-black factory finishes? Is there published support for a
reflectance FLOOR — i.e. that real black finishes do not go below some sRGB value —
and what is that value?

7. What batch-to-batch and inter-sheen colour tolerance (ΔE00 or ΔE*ab) do interior
paint manufacturers publish or accept? This calibrates whether a pass ≤1.0 /
warn ≤2.0 gate against a swatch-derived anchor is achievable in practice or is
tighter than the industry's own tolerance.

8. Do any of the Thai brands above publish spectral or colorimetric data (L*a*b*,
LRV) in a machine-readable form — a downloadable fan-deck data file, an API, or a
colour-tool export? Name the exact URL if so.

### 1. Thai-Market Paint Brands (TOA, Beger, Jotun, Nippon)
* **Thai-market interior emulsion lines (TOA, Beger, Jotun Thailand, Nippon Paint Thailand):** **NOT IN SOURCES** (or **NO SOURCED VALUE FOUND**). None of these manufacturers or their specific local paint lines are mentioned in any of the provided documents. 

However, the sources contain detailed colorimetric and reflectance coordinates for global and heritage cream and off-white paint formulations in the roughly \\(75 - 90\%\\) Light Reflectance Value (LRV) band:
* **Wimborne White (No. 239)** (*Farrow & Ball*): Published LRV is **\\(89.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((244, 240, 229)\\)** (Hex **#F4F0E5**) [1].
* **Pointing (No. 2003)** (*Farrow & Ball*): Published LRV is **\\(88.19\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((247, 241, 227)\\)** (Hex **#F7F1E3**) [1, 2].
* **Natural White (SW1F4)** (*Dulux*): Published LRV is **\\(85.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((238, 236, 229)\\)** (Hex **#EEECE5**) [1] (also published as LRV **\\(85\\)**, Hex **#eeece5** [3]).
* **Antique White (SW1H7)** (*Dulux*): Published LRV is **\\(84.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((239, 234, 224)\\)** (Hex **#EFEAE0**) [1] (also published as LRV **\\(84\\)**, Hex **#efeae0** [4]).
* **Alabaster (SW 7008)** (*Sherwin-Williams*): Published LRV is **\\(82.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((237, 235, 226)\\)** (Hex **#EDEBE2**) [1].
* **Swiss Coffee (OC-45)** (*Benjamin Moore*): Published LRV is **\\(81.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((238, 236, 225)\\)** (Hex **#EEECE1**) [1].
* **Slipper Satin (No. 2004)** (*Farrow & Ball*): 
  * *Discrepancy:* *Quantitative Modeling...* lists its LRV at **\\(74.16\%\\)** with sRGB **\\((232, 224, 209)\\)** (Hex **#E8E0D1**) [1], matching *DesignShop* [5]. However, *Housepaint AI* lists its LRV at **\\(75\%\\)** with sRGB **\\((230, 224, 210)\\)** (Hex **#E6E0D2**) [6].
* **Shoji White (SW 7042)** (*Sherwin-Williams*): Published LRV is **\\(74.00\%\\)** with an actual chromatic sRGB of **\\((231, 226, 215)\\)** (Hex **#E7E2D7**) [1].

*Source Titles:* 
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"* 
* *"Natural White (Dulux): What Color Is, Review, and Use - Hackrea"*
* *"Antique White U.S.A. (Dulux): What Color Is, Review, and Use - Hackrea"*
* *"Slipper Satin 2004 by Farrow & Ball | Paint Color | Housepaint AI"*
* *"Slipper Satin - DesignShop"*

---

### 2. Paint LRV vs. CIE Luminance Y & sRGB Derivation
* **Relationship between Paint LRV and CIE Luminance Y:** For a perfectly neutral, achromatic paint formulation, the normalized CIE 1931 tristimulus value \\(Y\\) (luminance) is directly equivalent to the normalized LRV [7]:
  \\[Y = \frac{\text{LRV}}{100.0}\\]
* **Achromatic sRGB Derivation Procedure:** Under perfectly achromatic conditions, the normalized linear red, green, and blue components (\\(R_{\text{linear}}\\), \\(G_{\text{linear}}\\), \\(B_{\text{linear}}\\)) are equal to the normalized luminance \\(Y\\) [7]:
  \\[R_{\text{linear}} = G_{\text{linear}} = B_{\text{linear}} = Y\\]
  To obtain standard, non-linear sRGB coordinates, the opto-electronic transfer function (OETF) defined by the sRGB standard (IEC 61966-2-1) is applied to each channel (\\(C_{\text{linear}}\\)) [8]:
  \\[\text{If } C_{\text{linear}} \le 0.0031308: C_{\text{sRGB}} = 12.92 \times C_{\text{linear}}\\]
  \\[\text{Else: } C_{\text{sRGB}} = 1.055 \times \left( C_{\text{linear}}^{\frac{1}{2.4}} \right) - 0.055\\]
  The resulting non-linear sRGB values are then scaled to standard 8-bit integers (\\([9]\\)) [8, 10]:
  \\[C_{\text{8bit}} = \text{round}\left( C_{\text{sRGB}} \times 255 \right)\\]
* **Chromatic sRGB Derivation from LRV + Hue Description:** **NO SOURCED VALUE FOUND** (or **NOT IN SOURCES**). The sources do not document a standardized mathematical procedure to derive a chromatic sRGB triple from a descriptive hue name combined with an LRV. Instead, they note that chromatic paint formulations rely on precise, non-linear pigment loading ratios that must be physically measured with a spectrophotometer [11].

*Source Titles:* 
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"*
* *"Physically Based Rendering in Filament - Google"*

---

### 3. White Oak Veneer (Lacquered vs. Oiled)
The physical and optical parameters reported for White/European oak veneer in scan-based libraries and published references under differing treatments are as follows:

#### (a) Under Clear Matte Lacquer (Continuous Surface Film)
* **Base Color / Albedo:** Saturated golden-brown tones; high visual contrast; warm grain bands [12].
* **Microfacet Roughness:** Low-to-moderate base roughness of **\\(0.15 - 0.35\\)** beneath the coat layer [12].
* **Coat Weight:** **\\(1.0\\)** (Continuous polymer film layer) [12].
* **Coat Roughness:** Very low, ranging between **\\(0.05 - 0.15\\)** [12].
* **Index of Refraction (IOR):** **\\(1.49 - 1.55\\)** (representing acrylic/polyurethane boundaries) [12].
* **Anisotropy Weight:** Minimal, ranging between **\\(0.00 - 0.15\\)** (as it is masked by the clear coat film) [12].
* **Normal Map Detail:** Smooth, high-frequency surface ripples [12].

#### (b) Under Penetrating Hardwax Oil (No Surface Film)
* **Base Color / Albedo:** Neutral light beige to cream tones; soft, low-contrast grain patterns [12].
* **Microfacet Roughness:** High-to-very-high microfacet roughness of **\\(0.40 - 0.65\\)** (yielding a highly tactile, raw feel) [12].
* **Coat Weight:** **\\(0.0\\)** (indicating no surface film layer is present) [12].
* **Index of Refraction (IOR):** **\\(1.45 - 1.50\\)** (representing the wood cellulose/lignin oil boundary) [12].
* **Anisotropy Weight:** Moderate-to-high, ranging between **\\(0.30 - 0.60\\)** (aligned along the grain path) [12].
* **Normal Map Detail:** Deep micro-pores and open cellular cracks [12].

#### Named Scan-Based Material Libraries & Procedural Shading Tools:
* **3DCollective** (*PBR Wood Materials Pack 01*): Captured from physical boards measuring up to \\(250 \times 150\text{ cm}\\) using cross-polarization at \\(32\text{K}\\) resolution (URL: `https://3dcollective.es/en/producto/wood-pack-01/`) [13-15].
* **Poliigon** (*Slip Match Oak Wood Veneer Texture*): Scanned physical white oak boards delivering ORM maps up to \\(32\text{ px/cm}\\) texel density (URL: `https://www.poliigon.com/texture/slip-match-oak-wood-veneer-texture/7760`) [13, 16].
* **CGAxis** (*Washed Oak Wood PBR Texture*): Standard PBR texture stack (URL: `https://cgaxis.com/product/washed-oak-wood-pbr-texture/`) [17, 18].
* **Substance Player / Wood Builder** (*ChiefTalk Forum*): Procedural shading tool utilizing White Oak, White Oak Quartersawn, and White Oak Rift Sawn inputs (URL: `https://chieftalk.chiefarchitect.com/topic/21560-custom-material-generation-with-substance-player/`) [13, 19].

*Source Titles:*
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"*
* *"Wood Materials Pack 01 | 3DCollective"*
* *"Custom Material Generation with Substance Player - ChiefTalk Forum - Chief Architect"*

### 4. Architectural Powder-Coat Black & GU-to-Roughness Conversion
#### Published 60° Gloss-Unit (GU) Bands:
* **Matte Black:**
  * **\\(0 - 20\text{ GU}\\)** (Source: *Choosing a Powder Coat Colour for a Vancouver Steel Stair* [20]).
  * **\\(25 \pm 5\text{ GU}\\)** (Source: *Drylac® Produktdatenblatt* [21, 22]).
  * **\\(< 30 \pm 5\text{ GU}\\)** (Category 1 Matt) (Source: *Epoxy Polyester Range - Online Paint Shop* [23]).
  * **\\(25 - 35\text{ GU}\\)** (IGP-HWFsuperior 5703) (Source: *IGP.FOR SURE.* [24]).
  * **\\(10 - 30\text{ GU}\\)** (Standard Matte), **\\(<10\text{ GU}\\)** (Super Matte/True Matte) (Source: *Powder Coating Matte Finish for Industrial Products* [25, 26]).
* **Satin Black:**
  * **\\(20 - 40\text{ GU}\\)** (Source: *Choosing a Powder Coat Colour for a Vancouver Steel Stair* [20]).
  * **\\(70 \pm 7\text{ GU}\\)** (Smooth Semi-Gloss) (Source: *Drylac® Produktdatenblatt* [21, 22]).
  * **\\(31 - 70 \pm 7\text{ GU}\\)** (Category 2 Semi-Gloss) (Source: *Epoxy Polyester Range - Online Paint Shop* [23]).
  * **\\(65 - 85\text{ GU}\\)** (IGP-HWFsuperior 5707 Silk Gloss) (Source: *IGP.FOR SURE.* [24]).
  * **\\(60 - 80\text{ GU}\\)** (Satin), **\\(30 - 60\text{ GU}\\)** (Semi-Matte) (Source: *Powder Coating Matte Finish for Industrial Products* [25, 26]).
* **Gloss Black:**
  * **\\(\ge 70\text{ GU}\\)** (Full Gloss) (Source: *Choosing a Powder Coat Colour for a Vancouver Steel Stair* [27]).
  * **\\(80 - 95\text{ GU}\\)** (Smooth Glossy) (Source: *Drylac® Produktdatenblatt* [21, 22]).
  * **\\(71 - 100 \pm 10\text{ GU}\\)** (Category 3 Full Gloss) (Source: *Epoxy Polyester Range - Online Paint Shop* [23]).
  * **\\(80 - 90+\text{ GU}\\)** (High Gloss) (Source: *Powder Coating Matte Finish for Industrial Products* [26] / *Interpon D1036 Gloss* [28]).

#### Sourced GU-to-Roughness Conversion:
In standard real-time PBR engines, physical \\(60^\circ\\) glossmeter readings (\\(GU\\)) are simplified and directly mapped to standard GGX microfacet roughness (\\(\alpha_{\text{GGX}}\\)) using the following mathematical relationships [29, 30]:
* **Standard GGX Roughness Mapping (\\(\alpha_{\text{GGX}}\\)):**
  \\[\alpha_{\text{GGX}} = \sqrt{1.0 - \frac{GU}{100}}\\]
* **Linear Roughness Parameter Mapping (\\(r\\)):**
  \\[r = 1.0 - \frac{GU}{100}\\]

* *"Choosing a Powder Coat Colour for a Vancouver Steel Stair"*

* *"Epoxy Polyester Range - Online Paint Shop"*
* *"IGP.FOR SURE."*

### 5. Electro-Optic Profiling of Brass Accents
#### Measured Complex Refractive Index (\\(n, k\\)) and \\(F_0\\):
At red (\\(650\text{ nm}\\)), green (\\(550\text{ nm}\\)), and blue (\\(450\text{ nm}\\)) wavelengths, measured constants are:
* **Real Refractive Index (\\(n\\)):** \\([0.444, 0.527, 1.094]\\) [31].
* **Extinction Coefficient (\\(k\\)):** \\([3.695, 2.765, 1.829]\\) [31].
* **Fresnel Reflectance at Normal Incidence (\\(F_0\\)):** \\([0.89, 0.79, 0.43]\\) (derived exactly from electromagnetic constants as \\([0.8872, 0.7887, 0.4339]\\)) [31-33].
* **Database Name:** *refractiveindex.info* ("selected data for 3D artists" database curated by Mikhail Polyanskiy) [33, 34].
* **Dynamic / Alternative Alloy Indices:** Ellipsometric modeling of aluminum-brass alloys under dynamic polarized solutions/cathodic oxidation yields a dynamic index of \\(n_s = 0.645 - 3.35i\\) [33, 35].

#### Discrepancies in Measured Material Databases for sRGB \\(F_0\\):
* **Standard Conductor Fit (derived from physical indexes):** Linear \\(F_0\\) converts to a non-linear sRGB base color of **\\([36-38]\\)** (Hex **#F2E6B0**) [33].
* **Filament Materials Guide / Real-Time Rendering 4th Edition Database:** Lists sRGB \\(f_0\\) for Brass as **\\([0.98, 0.90, 0.59]\\)** (Hex **#f9e596**) [39, 40].
* **OpenPBR F82-Tint Fit Database:** Lists sRGB \\(F_0\\) as **\\([0.962, 0.713, 0.464]\\)** and the silhouette F82-tint as **\\([0.971, 0.994, 1.019]\\)** [41].

#### PBR Parameter Ranges for Satin Brass Hardware [35]:
* **Base Color (RGB):** \\([36-38]\\) [35] (or \\([42-44]\\) [45]).
* **Metalness:** \\(1.0\\) (Conductor) [35].
* **Microfacet Roughness:** Moderate-to-high, ranging from **\\(0.20 - 0.35\\)** [35].
* **Anisotropy:** Moderate-to-high, ranging from **\\(0.40 - 0.70\\)** (representing parallel groove elongation) [35, 46].

*Source Titles:*
* *"A Polarizing Filter Function for Real-Time Rendering - Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques"*
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"*
* *"Physically Based Rendering in Filament - Google"*
* *"OpenPBR: Novel Features and Implementation Details - arXiv"*

### 6. Reflectance Floor for Real Black Finishes
* **Physical Reflectance Floor (LRV):** The most carbon-dense, light-absorbent black paints typically register at approximately **\\(5\%\\) LRV** [47]. Converting 5% LRV (\\(Y = 0.05\\)) through the non-linear sRGB transfer function yields an achromatic 8-bit sRGB value of **\\((63, 63, 63)\\)** (Hex **#3F3F3F**) [7, 8, 10].
* **PBR Shading Floor Guidelines:** To prevent artists from authoring physically impossible "black-hole" materials, standard PBR guides publish a strict reflectance floor for non-metallic base colors:
  * **Strict Range Floor:** **sRGB \\(50\\)** [48].
  * **Tolerant Range Floor:** **sRGB \\(30\\)** [48].
* **Measured Dielectric Standards:** Standard measured non-metallic black finishes do not go below these thresholds:
  * **Coal:** sRGB **\\([0.19, 0.19, 0.19]\\)** (Hex **#323232**) [49].
  * **Rubber:** sRGB **\\([0.21, 0.21, 0.21]\\)** (Hex **#353535**) [49].
* **Black Powder-Coat Finishes:** Modern black powder-coated elements with a matte finish typically feature an LRV of **\\(<10\%\\)** and a \\(60^\circ\\) gloss rating of \\(10 - 20\text{ GU}\\) (equivalent to standard GGX roughness of \\(\alpha_{\text{GGX}} \approx 0.89 - 0.95\\)) [50].

*Source Titles:*
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"*
* *"Physically Based Rendering in Filament - Google"*
* *"Filament Materials Guide - Google"*

---

### 7. Paint Industry Color Tolerances
Published and accepted color difference limits (CIE \\(\Delta E_{ab}^*\\) or \\(\Delta E_{00}\\)) are categorized as follows:
* **Batch-to-Batch Tolerances:**
  * **Standard Opaque/Solid Paints:** Manufactured to an extremely tight batch limit of **\\(\Delta E \le 1.0\\)** [51], which represents the absolute limit of trained human visual perception under close, side-by-side comparison [52, 53]. 
  * **General Architectural / Solid Coatings Industry Standard:** Maximum allowable batch-to-batch variation is **\\(\Delta E \le 2.0\\)** (specified in AAMA 2605) [51, 54, 55].
  * **Mica, Flake, or Metallic Powder Coatings:** Batch tolerance increases to **\\(\Delta E \le 2.5\\)** [56] due to the angle-dependent reflectivity ("flop index") of aluminum or mica flakes suspended in the binder [57, 58]. 
  * **Metallic Flake Working Tolerance:** Cumulative process and substrate variables yield a real-world working tolerance of **\\(\Delta E \le 0.5\\)** [52].
* **High-Regulation Rejection Thresholds:** High-regulation industries (such as automotive, consumer electronics, or critical architectural matching) reject batches when **\\(\Delta E > 1.0\\)** [51, 59].
* **Weathering / Environmental Fade Tolerance:** Standard architectural warranties (AAMA 2604 and AAMA 2605) guarantee color fastness against weathering up to a maximum fade limit of **\\(\Delta E \le 5.0\\)** over 5-year and 10-year outdoor exposure periods respectively [51, 60, 61].

#### Evaluation of the \\(\Delta E\\) Gate:
A pass gate of **\\(\le 1.0\\)** is achievable for solid opaque cream paint, but represents the extreme edge of manufacturing capability [51, 62]. A warn gate of **\\(\le 2.0\\)** is realistic and aligns with architectural standards [51, 54]. For metallic finishes, a \\(\Delta E \le 1.0\\) pass gate is physically unachievable due to flake orientation variations [14, 52].

*Source Titles:*
* *"Quantitative Modeling of Cream, White Oak, and Black Architectural Palettes: A Comprehensive PBR and Optical Materials Report"*
* *"Controlling Variation in a Paint Color - Linetec"*
* *"How is color measured? - Calculating Delta E - ALPOLIC"*
* *"Visual Perception of Metallic Paint on Reynobond® panels Technical Bulletin | Arconic"*
* *"How to Ensure Accurate Color in Building Materials-3NH - Threenh"*
* *"What Is Delta E (ΔE)? Understanding Colour Difference in Quality Control"*

---

### 8. Thai Brands Machine-Readable Color Data
* **Machine-readable files, APIs, or exports by Thai paint brands (TOA, Beger, Jotun Thailand, Nippon Paint Thailand):** **NOT IN SOURCES** (or **NO SOURCED VALUE FOUND**). 

None of the Thai paint manufacturers are represented in any capacity in the provided documents. The only paint data compilation tools mentioned are:
* **The Paint Color DNA Studio Table** (`thelandofcolor.com/color-dna-studio`): A database compiling the LRV, hue angle, chroma, and value notations for major North American and European manufacturers [63, 64].
* **EasyRGB** (`easyrgb.com`): A recommended web tool for comparing relative color data and extracting consistent Light Reflectance Values across mainstream paint brands [65].

*Source Titles:* 
* *"LRV - The Best Guide for Paint Colors and More! - The Land of Color"*
